summary: Rock-pile country on the Burrup Peninsula near Dampier, holding one of the largest, densest and most diverse collections of rock engravings in the world: an estimated one to two million petroglyphs across the Murujuga Cultural Landscape, inscribed as World Heritage in 2025. Murujuga National Park, 5,134 hectares, is Aboriginal land owned by the Murujuga Aboriginal Corporation and was Western Australia's first jointly managed national park. Most visitors walk the short Nganjarli (Deep Gorge) trail. Entry is free.
story: Murujuga is made mostly of granophyre, a fine-grained granite, and gabbro, which pushed in as a sheet of magma at least two kilometres thick about 2.7 billion years ago. Both resist erosion, and as they broke down they left the park's extraordinary rock piles, oxidised over thousands of years to a deep red; a freshly split rock is blue-grey inside. The Dampier Archipelago formed only 5,000 to 6,000 years ago, when the sea rose after the last ice age and drowned a hilly landscape, leaving its hilltops as islands. Murujuga, in the Ngarluma-Yaburara language, means 'hip bone sticking out'.

The rock piles are habitats in their own right. Moisture gathers among them, sheltering plants with Kimberley affinities such as the native rock fig, and Pilbara specialities like the rock kurrajong. Rock pools, some near-permanent and fed by seepage, hold small fish and invertebrates. More than 14 native mammals, 14 bat species and 58 reptiles live here, including Rothschild's rock-wallaby and the Pilbara olive python, one of Australia's largest snakes. Mangroves and mudflats edge the coast, and thousands of migratory shorebirds visit each spring and summer.

The Ngarda-Ngarli, the collective name of the Ngarluma, Yindjibarndi, Yaburara, Mardudhunera and Wong-Goo-Tt-Oo peoples, have been part of Murujuga for tens of thousands of years. Their engravings show human figures, extinct animals such as thylacines and megafauna, and the birds, fish and animals still found here, some estimated at more than 47,000 years old. With shell middens, grinding stones, fish traps, rock shelters and stone arrangements, they record continuous care and use of the area for over 50,000 years, and they still link people to stories, customs and knowledge of their land.

Murujuga National Park was created in January 2013 as Western Australia's 100th national park. The Dampier Archipelago, including the park, was placed on the National Heritage List in 2007. A nomination led by the Murujuga Aboriginal Corporation on behalf of the Ngarda-Ngarli, with the Western Australian government and the support of the Australian Government, led to the Murujuga Cultural Landscape being inscribed on the World Heritage List on 11 July 2025, Australia's 21st World Heritage site.
howItWorks: Murujuga National Park is Aboriginal land. It is held as freehold by the Murujuga Aboriginal Corporation (MAC), which represents the five Traditional Owner groups, and is leased back to the Western Australian Government. It is jointly managed by MAC and the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA), the first jointly managed national park in WA, through the Murujuga Park Council, on which DBCA's Parks and Wildlife Service, MAC and the Department of Planning, Lands and Heritage sit. Over the long term, the Ngarda-Ngarli seek to manage the park with greater independence. MAC's rangers patrol and work across the park alongside DBCA.

Entry to the park is free, and there is no camping in it. The main visitor site is Nganjarli (Deep Gorge), off Hearson Cove Road, where a 700-metre wheelchair-accessible loop of paths, ramps and boardwalk leads past engravings, a shell midden and grinding stones. MAC offers cultural tours and cultural awareness sessions. The nearest toilets, barbecues and shelters are at Hearson Cove beach, which is outside the park and run by the City of Karratha; fresh water is not available in the park.

The Murujuga Elders ask visitors not to photograph or film rock art depicting humanoid figures and faces, not to take home rocks or other natural items, and not to climb on the rock piles, which can be unstable and are a physical and cultural safety hazard. Report any damage to Aboriginal sites or rock art to MAC or the Department of Planning, Lands and Heritage. Pets are not allowed: 1080 baits are laid in and around the park to control foxes and feral cats.

sights.name: Nganjarli (Deep Gorge)
sights.note: A 700-metre wheelchair-accessible loop past petroglyphs, a shell midden, grinding stones and medicine plants, with interpretive panels. Best in early morning or late afternoon, when shadows bring out the engravings.

sights.name: Burrup Peninsula rock piles
sights.note: The red granophyre and gabbro rock piles that cover the peninsula, home to rock figs, rock pools and Rothschild's rock-wallabies. Admire them from the ground: do not climb.

entrances: Hearson Cove Road on the Burrup Peninsula, near Dampier and Karratha, for Nganjarli (Deep Gorge)
By boat to the park's beaches; the informal ramp at Withnell Bay is outside the park, and there are two ramps in Dampier
planYourVisit.reservations: No booking or entry fee. Book Aboriginal cultural tours with the Murujuga Aboriginal Corporation (experiencemurujuga.com). Check DBCA Park Alerts before you go.
permits: None for general visits; commercial activities need permission from DBCA
camping: Camping is not permitted in Murujuga National Park
seasonalClosures: Hiking is recommended only in the cool season, April to October; temperatures can exceed 50°C from November to April

weather: Murujuga lies on the western edge of the semi-desert tropical Pilbara, and the Ngarluma and Yindjibarndi recognise two seasons: the cold time, Muthu, from April to October, and the hot time, Garrbarn or Garrwarn, from November to March. The sea, never more than two kilometres away, makes the peninsula cooler and more humid than the inland Pilbara, but temperatures can still exceed 50°C from November to April. Most significant rain falls between November and April, from tropical cyclones and scattered summer thunderstorms, and bushfires can start at any time of year.
directions: Murujuga is on the Burrup Peninsula in the Pilbara, near the towns of Dampier and Karratha; the Parks and Wildlife Service's Pilbara office is in Karratha. Nganjarli (Deep Gorge) is off Hearson Cove Road. Access roads north of Withnell Bay are extremely rough and normally need a high-clearance or four-wheel-drive vehicle, and beach tracks near the water depend on the tide. Many of the park's beaches can also be reached by boat.

fees.title: Park entry
fees.detail: Murujuga is not among the WA parks with entry fees. As listed by DBCA in November 2026.

chronology.text: The granophyre and gabbro of Murujuga form from a sheet of magma.
The oldest engravings at Nganjarli are made, part of a record of human care for the area spanning more than 50,000 years.
Rising seas drown the hills, forming the Dampier Archipelago.
The Dampier Archipelago, including the Burrup Peninsula, is placed on the National Heritage List.
Murujuga National Park is created in January as WA's 100th national park and its first jointly managed one.
The Murujuga Cultural Landscape is inscribed on the World Heritage List on 11 July.

safety: Temperatures can exceed 50°C from November to April. Hike in the cooler months, carry and drink at least a litre of water per hour, and finish before dark; there is no drinking water in the park.
Do not climb the rock piles: rocks can be unstable.
Saltwater crocodiles are occasionally seen; take care launching boats. Stinging jellyfish occur in summer.
Bushfires can start without warning at any time of year. If you see or smell smoke, move to safety and call 000 and the Parks and Wildlife Service Pilbara Region on (08) 9182 2000.
Mobile reception is good in most areas, especially on high ground; install the Emergency+ app before you go.
regulations: Do not photograph or film rock art depicting humanoid figures and faces, as the Murujuga Elders request.
Do not take rocks or other natural items, or touch or damage rock art and cultural sites.
No pets: 1080 baits are laid in and around the park.
